newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - Sri Lanka city struggles for normal life.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sri Lanka city struggles for normal life.

text.p: The young Sinhalese soldier grips his automatic rifle nervously, checks his flak jacket and stares watchfully at the passing Tamils outside the van.
In the long-running ethnic war that has ravaged this Indian Ocean island, an attack can come from anywhere.
The Sri Lankan army has held this northern city for a year, having taken it from the Tigers after a huge offensive.
It is slowly cementing its control over the stronghold which the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) held for most of the past 13 years.
Clashes are rarer now in Jaffna, but occasionally one of what the army says is a dwindling number of Tamil Tigers within its zone will lob a grenade into a passing military vehicle.
Security remains tight, with checkpoints every 100 metres (yards). Makeshift barricades, bunkers and guard posts are everywhere.

But, increasingly, the army is turning its attention to restoring essential services, such as power, and overcoming the devastation of 13 years of war, said a senior military official, who did not want to be identified.
At the small but bustling market in the centre of Jaffna, Randasamy Shivayoyogi says things aren't happening fast enough.
Restrictions on fishing activities -- imposed for security reasons -- are limiting supplies, said the 56-year-old fishmonger, poking at a few remaining crabs and squid.
"Because of the (restrictions) I can't get enough fish," she said.
Shoppers complain of inflated prices and a shortage of many items.
The constant security checks and lack of public transport make normal life impossible, said a teacher who did not want to give his name.
"It is very difficult, public transport is a real problem," he said.

Once a thriving tropical city, Jaffna is littered with ruins and roads badly in need of repair -- the 35-km (20 mile) drive from Palaly airbase takes almost an hour as potholes slow vehicles to a crawl.
What buildings remain standing are marked by bullet-holes, bomb damage and other scars of war.
The city is under curfew from 8.00 p.m. until 5.30 a.m., although with no electricity and no entertainment, the streets are largely deserted when darkness falls.
People remain guarded in their public conversations with strangers, among so many soldiers.
"Business people are afraid to talk," one shopowner said.
